Nestlings of the Wedge-tailed shearwater hatch after an incubation period lasting 53 days [ab = 53 days] when the egg is maintained at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns with the prolonged development typical for procellariiform seabirds. Upon emerging from the calcareous egg, the altricial chick weighs a modest 60 grams [Wwb = 60 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves required for the final stages of embryogenesis. This initial body mass is followed by a period of rapid mass gain driven by frequent parental provisioning of lipid-rich stomach oil and partially digested fish. Field studies on Heron Island indicate that the growing juvenile attains a maximum adult body mass of 474.6 grams [Wwi = 474.6 grams] by the time it achieves full somatic independence, a figure consistent with the upper range reported for tropical populations of this species.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the active metabolic phase in this seabird, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the fledgling achieves its first sustained flight at 109 days after hatching [tx = 109 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone marks the transition from a nest-dependent chick to an independent juvenile capable of foraging over pelagic waters. The fledging period is closely tied to the accumulation of adequate lipid stores, which buffer the young bird against the energetic demands of initial flight and the subsequent period of learning to catch prey. Interestingly, some sources report a broader range for this trait, with fledging occurring anywhere from 103 to 115 days after hatching (103-115 days after hatching) [tx = 103-115 days after hatching] depending on local food availability and individual growth trajectories at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. The variation in this key life-history event underscores the sensitivity of developmental timing to both intrinsic physiological condition and extrinsic environmental factors.

Sexual maturation in Ardenna pacifica proceeds at a deliberate pace, with puberty reached at 327 days after hatching [tp = 327 days after hatching] when the individual is experiencing the core body temperature typical of active metabolism, around 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This timing for the onset of gonadal activity is notably slower than that observed in many smaller petrels and shearwaters, a pattern that may reflect the energetic priority placed on completing skeletal and muscular growth before diverting resources toward gametogenesis. The development of functional reproductive organs entails a suite of endocrinological changes, including a surge in circulating testosterone in males and estradiol in females, which ultimately triggers the enlargement of the gonads and the initiation of spermatogenesis and follicular development. Males, in particular, exhibit a slightly lower asymptotic body mass of 457 grams [Wwi = 457 grams] at this stage, indicating a subtle sexual dimorphism in overall size that may influence competitive interactions during the subsequent breeding season.

The age at which a Wedge-tailed shearwater first successfully raises a brood is a critical demographic parameter, and data from recapture studies on the Great Barrier Reef show that the time since birth at first brood is 4 years [tR = 4 years] under the thermal conditions of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] that correspond to active metabolic rates. This delayed onset of reproduction is a hallmark of long-lived seabirds, which typically require several years to acquire the foraging proficiency, body condition, and social experience necessary to compete for burrow sites and successfully incubate a single egg. The interval between hatching and first breeding is thus a period of intense learning, during which young birds refine their aerial and underwater hunting skills. In some populations, first reproduction may be deferred for an additional year, particularly if oceanic conditions are unfavorable and prey resources are scarce, highlighting the plasticity of this trait in the face of environmental variability.

The maximum lifespan documented for the Wedge-tailed shearwater in the wild reaches 29 years [am = 29 years] at a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a longevity that places it among the more durable members of the Procellariidae. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a characteristically low annual reproductive output; for instance, a typical breeding pair produces a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and raises only one brood each year [F_R_i = one brood each year]. The combination of high adult survival and modest fecundity is a classic K-selected life-history strategy that buffers populations against the vagaries of unpredictable pelagic food supplies. The extreme longevity also means that mature individuals can accumulate substantial reproductive experience, with older breeders consistently showing higher hatching success and chick fledging rates compared to younger, less experienced birds attempting their first nesting attempt.
